item.title: Cell Alert in Switzerland: 16 million approved
item.description: Federal Council requires CHF 15.8 million per cell broadcast. New alarm system that sends SMS directly to phones in the affected area.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Commitment credit of CHF 15.8 million for cell broadcast system - Urgent SMS alert to mobile phones in the affected area - Implementation timeline from 2027 to 2035
## Key facts - **What**: Cell broadcast alarm system that sends SMS to phones - When: Credit application in 2026; implementation 2027–2035 - Where: All of Switzerland - Who: Federal Council to Federal Parliament - Amount: 15.8 million CHF commitment credit; 67.7 million total 2027–2035 - Infrastructure: at national telephone operators - Support: Cantons and Parliament have requested acceleration
The Federal Council has sent Parliament a request for a commitment appropriation of CHF 15.8 million to implement a new alarm system called "cell broadcast". This system allows you to send short text messages directly to mobile phones in an affected area in the event of an alarm or urgent alert.
Unlike sirens, which reach an audience limited to urban areas, cell broadcasting offers widespread coverage of the national territory through the infrastructure network of telecommunications providers. The new channel complements and reinforces the civil protection devices already in operation: traditional sirens, radio releases subject to the broadcasting obligation, as well as the Alertswiss website and app, which have been active since 2018.
### Project Acceleration and Federal Consent
The Board ## # How cell broadcasting works nationwide
Cell broadcasting represents a significant evolution in the federal civil protection strategy. Unlike alarm sirens, which require geographical proximity and direct visibility to function effectively, the cell broadcast sends short, automatic text messages directly to the mobile phones of those in the affected area at that specific time.
This approach does not require the receiver to have a special subscription, to have installed an app, to have activated a notification service or to be listening to a radio. The system operates at the national telephone network infrastructure level: when a federal or cantonal authority authorizes the sending of an alarm, the text message automatically reaches all phones connected to the telephone cells in the affected area, regardless of the network provider chosen.
### Multi-channel integration: redundancy and resilience
The strategic importance of cell broadcasting lies not in the replacement of existing systems, but in their integration. The sirens remain operational for immediate visual and auditory alarm in urban and peri-urban areas. Radio announcements subject to the broadcasting obligation continue to provide detailed and contextual information on an ongoing alarm. The Alertswiss app, active since 2018, allows residents to proactively search for alarm information

item.title: Global environment: 176 million from Switzerland until 2030
item.description: The Federal Council approves a commitment appropriation of CHF 176.23 million to finance international environmental projects from 2027 to 2030, but Parliament will have to approve it.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Federal Council approves CHF 176.23 million for global environment (2027-2030) - 21 million less than the 2023-2026 period due to federal savings - Parliament will have to give final approval to the commitment credit - Funds earmarked for the Global Environment Facility, ozone, climate adaptation
## Key facts - **Amount**: CHF 176.23 million - Period: 2027-2030 - Who: Federal Council (approval); Parliament (ratification) - Comparison: 21 million less than 2023-2026 - Reason: Savings measures of the Confederation - Main recipient: Global Environment Facility (132.1 million)
The Federal Council has approved a commitment credit of CHF 176.23 million to finance environmental protection projects globally between 2027 and 2030. It is a decision that reflects Bern's priorities in the fight against global climate degradation, but also represents a significant cut compared to previous funding.
Comparison with the past: between 2023 and 2026, the Confederation allocated about 197 million francs for the same objectives. The reduction of about 21 million stems from the savings measures announced by the federal government. The executive stresses that international funding in the environmental sector remains critical, given the continued degradation of the global climate and the imperative need to act.
### Fund allocations
The preponderant part of the credit, 132.1 ### The Trade-off Between Environment and Defense
The Federal Council's decision on environmental financing is part of a broader context of federal spending redistribution. Last week, the government announced a budget surplus of 800 million francs for 2026 (instead of the previously expected deficit), but simultaneously requested a supplementary investment of 970 million for the military.
This framework reveals the executive's priorities: on one hand, fiscal consolidation; on the other, strengthening the Confederation's defensive capacity. In between, international financing for the environment is experiencing erosion compared to the previous four-year period.
### Meaning of the Reduction
The cut of 21 million between the two four-year periods (2023-2026 vs 2027-2030) corresponds to approximately 10% of Switzerland's international environmental spending. Although the size of the cut may appear modest in absolute terms, it signals a change in approach: the Confederation continues to finance global environmental protection, but with decreasing resources.
### Switzerland's Role in Environmental Cooperation
Switzerland is traditionally active in environmental diplomacy and international climate financing. The Global Environment Facility (GEF), the principal beneficiary of this credit, is a crucial instrument for transferring resources from developed countries to developing ones, accelerating the ecological transition in vulnerable economies.
At the same time, the Federal Council is asking the Swiss private sector to invest more in environmental protection. This request reflects a model of shared responsibility: public financing provides the foundation, but innovation and the scale of change also depend on private capital.
### Implications for Taxpayers and Policy
For Swiss taxpayers, this means that a portion of federal tax revenue will continue to finance environmental projects abroad, albeit in slightly lower amounts. Understanding the burden of [federal taxation](nav:calculator) and how the government employs it is essential for monitoring the Confederation's spending priorities. At the national policy-making level, parliamentary debate on this credit appropriation will offer an opportunity for broader discussion on Switzerland's external climate strategy and the balance between domestic and international interventions.

The procedure is clear: the Federal Council has already taken its step. Now the budget allocation must pass through the Federal Parliament, where it will be debated by both chambers' committees (National Council and Council of States) and, if necessary, the plenary assembly. The final vote will determine whether Switzerland will proceed with financing in the 2027-2030 four-year period.
No exact date has been communicated for the parliamentary vote, but budget allocations of this nature are typically submitted to Parliament within a few months of government deliberation. item.title: Federal Council approves SECO-IMF partnership for economy
item.description: On 26 August, the Swiss Government allocated CHF 40 million for the SECO-FMI 2026-2030 programme, strengthening global economic institutions for the benefit of Swiss businesses.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Federal Council approves CHF 40 million for SECO-IMF partnership 2026-2030 - Strengthens finance ministries, central banks, supervisory authorities in partner countries - Benefits Swiss enterprises and investors through stable global markets
## Key facts - **What**: SECO-IMF partnership for international economic technical assistance - When: August 26, 2026 (duration 2026-2030) - Where: IMF partner countries worldwide - Who: Federal Council, SECO, IMF - Amount: CHF 40 million - Focus: Finance ministries, central banks, supervisory authorities, public debt management
August 26, 2026 — The Federal Council has approved an allocation of CHF 40 million for a new partnership between the State Secretariat for the Economy (SECO) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), valid from 2026 to 2030. The decision represents a significant commitment by Switzerland in strengthening global economic institutions through a targeted program of technical assistance to IMF member countries.
### Objectives and areas of intervention
The program focuses on three operational pillars: strengthening finance ministries, central banks, and financial supervisory authorities in partner countries; promoting sustainable management of public finances and debt; increasing the stability of financial sectors. A fourth crucial element concerns strengthening the integrity of financial systems and the provision of reliable economic data, a fundamental element for transparency in international financial markets.
These objectives are not abstract. Weak central banks, fragmented finance ministries, or ineffective supervisory authorities create economic instability that spreads rapidly through global financial flows. Switzerland, with an economic base strongly oriented towards international trade and cross-border investments, directly suffers the consequences of this instability.
### Direct and indirect benefits for Switzerland
Although the financing is directed at IMF partner countries, Switzerland and its [enterprises that employ](nav:companies) derive concrete benefits. Stable economic framework conditions facilitate market access, improve conditions for trade and investments, and reduce economic risks for Swiss operators. This investment is directly inscribed in Switzerland's foreign policy strategy and international cooperation program 2025-2028. ### Why Switzerland invests in global institutional stability
Switzerland does not operate in isolation in the global economic system. Weak and non-transparent international financial institutions are a source of systemic risk for developed economies. When an IMF partner country experiences a banking crisis or unsustainable public debt management, the effects spread rapidly through international trade and financial channels, also affecting Swiss companies and investors. Investing in technical assistance to strengthen sound finance ministries, credible central banks and transparent supervisory systems means protecting national economic interests in the long term.
The CHF 40 million allocated over the five-year period (approximately CHF 8 million annually) is therefore not a cost, but an investment in the prevention of global economic crises that would have incomparably higher costs if they were to occur.
### Swiss positioning in the Bretton Woods institutions
The new partnership further consolidates Switzerland's position in the core institutions of the global financial system: the IMF and the World Bank. Both organizations operate according to the weighted voting system, where Switzerland leads a voting group that includes several countries. Robust and credible technical assistance to member countries strengthens Switzerland's credibility in the international political-economic dialogue,

SECO, as the State Secretariat responsible for the economy, international trade, and financial affairs, manages the operational relationship with the IMF and the practical implementation of the program. The CHF 40 million financing will be allocated primarily to Swiss experts and consultants who will support IMF technicians in beneficiary countries, working directly within finance ministries, central banks, and local supervisory agencies. These experts often come from the Swiss federal administration, universities, and Swiss private consulting firms, creating employment opportunities for Swiss professionals in the financial and economic sectors.
SECO coordinates the program in coherence with the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA) and with Swiss bilateral cooperation agencies, ensuring that technical assistance is consistent with sustainable development programs and international cooperation already underway in many partner countries.
### Timeline and Monitoring
The program is officially valid from 2026 to 2030. During this five-year period, SECO and the IMF will share regular reports on progress, results achieved in beneficiary economic institutions (regulatory reforms implemented, institutional capacity strengthened, financial transparency improved) and benefits derived for the Swiss economy. In an interview with Tages-Anzeiger online, Wyss (59, in office since April) rejected criticism that raising prices while trains are crowded represents a contradiction. "The tariffs are not only set by the SBB," he said, "but by the entire industry."
The president, who boasts previous experiences as CEO of Implenia (construction giant) and background in chemical-pharmaceutical, stressed how the Railways have maintained stable prices for a long time despite inflation and increased operating costs. “We've kept prices stable for a long time, despite inflation and rising costs weighing on us as well,” says Wyss.

item.title: Record income and savings: the Swiss in 2025
item.description: Disposable income of CHF 65,124 per inhabitant in 2025. UST: voluntary savings rate rises to 19.3%, the highest in the Swiss statistical series.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Swiss disposable income reaches CHF 65,124 per inhabitant in 2025 (historical record) - Voluntary savings rate at 19.3%: maximum of the UST statistical series - Real growth of 36% since 1995: spending capacity never so strong - Disparities remain: housing and sick pay weigh on many families
## Key facts - **What**: Adjusted disposable income per Swiss citizen and voluntary savings rate - When: 2025 (data published by the UST with 2025 national accounts) - Where: Switzerland (national average) - Who: Federal Statistical Office (FSO) - Income: CHF 65,124 per inhabitant (first record in the series) - Voluntary savings: 19.3% of adjusted gross disposable income (new maximum) - Historical comparison: 36% real income growth since 1995 (then CHF 40,083)
For the first time, the adjusted disposable income per Swiss inhabitant exceeded CHF 65,000. In 2025, the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) published the national accounts confirming a historical economic milestone: the adjusted disposable income per inhabitant reached exactly CHF 65,124, the maximum of the entire available statistical series. Even more relevant is the figure on voluntary savings: in 2025 it reached 19.3% of adjusted gross disposable income, a new absolute record. Thirtyyears earlier, in 1995, this rate stood at 9.7%: today, therefore, the Swiss save almost twice as much as they did a generation ago.
The power ## Savings Rates: from Moderate to Historic Record
The savings behavior of the Swiss sets the country apart from many other developed nations. While in many countries, income increases generate mainly additional consumption, in Switzerland the opposite happens. In 2025, the overall savings rate (which includes both voluntary savings and mandatory pension contributions) was 27.4% of adjusted gross disposable income. In 1995 it was only 19.6%: an increase of almost 8 percentage points over three decades. This difference reflects a profound shift in the relationship between spending and wealth accumulation.
This propensity to save has not been constant over time. Between the late 1990s and the first decade of the 2000s, growth in savings was moderate. The real acceleration came during the COVID-19 pandemic, when consumption constraints (closures, travel restrictions, fear of economic uncertainty) forced families to accumulate resources. Once the health emergency ended, one might have expected a return to previous savings levels: instead the phenomenon has become established and rooted. Families continued to save significantly, a sign of financial soundness that has transformed into permanent economic behavior.
### Hidden Disparities in National Averages
UST data describes a national average and should not be misleading about the actual uniformity of Swiss economic well-being. Differences between regions, income brackets, and types of households remain significant. The increase in housing costs, [health insurance](nav:health) premiums, and other mandatory expenses continues to weigh heavily on many families. A couple with children in an expensive city (Zurich, Geneva, Lausanne, Basel) experiences economic pressures very different from those of a single-income family in rural areas or commuting zones. An increasingly large share of income is absorbed by rigid expenses.
UST data confirm that **real purchasing power has increased** at an aggregate level, but this does not mean even distribution. An average 36% growth since 1995 can mask very different realities: families that have fully benefited from Swiss economic prosperity, and others that have had to allocate increasingly larger percentages of income to fixed expenses (rents, [health insurance](nav:health) premiums, utilities, public services) leaving less room for discretionary savings.
### The Role of the Pension System
In interpreting this data, it is important to remember that the [Swiss pension system](nav:pension) (AVS/LPP) represents a significant component of overall savings behavior. A portion of "mandatory" savings falls within pension contributions according to the three-pillar system: the first public pillar (AVS) and the second occupational pillar (LPP) are mandatory for employees. Margins of voluntary savings (19.3% in 2025) reflect wealth accumulation choices beyond the legal minimum, a sign of confidence in one's future economic situation and capacity for long-term planning.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to Plan Your Savings in Switzerland
UST data provides a statistical snapshot, but true relevance is individual and personal. If you are a person working in Switzerland and planning your financial future, this historical trend of economic solidity opens new concrete possibilities. The first step is understanding how your personal disposable income is structured and where to allocate resources strategically, not randomly.
### Step 1: Verify your real disposable income
Calculate your gross income (base salary + bonuses), subtract federal, cantonal and municipal taxes, AVS/AI/IPG contributions (5.3% from employee, employer pays additional 5.3%), mandatory health insurance premiums, and consider the net value of public services you use (subsidized transportation, school, healthcare). The result is an estimate of your real disposable income, the "money that actually remains" each month after fixed institutional expenses. Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) for this initial estimate, then refine with your personal numbers.
### Step 2: Analyze your concrete mandatory expenses
The increase in [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) in Switzerland impacts especially three items that erode the savings margin:
- Rent and real estate: in Switzerland they account for 25-35% of disposable income in major cities (Zurich, Geneva, Lausanne, Basel) - Health insurance premiums: vary enormously by canton, age group and household (from CHF 200–600 monthly per person depending on deductible and provider) - Utilities and essential expenses: heating, electricity, internet, public and private transportation
If these three items absorb more than 50-60% of your disposable income, the savings margin is narrow regardless of the national average data cited by UST. National record savings rates (19.3%) do not apply uniformly to all demographic segments. Be honest in evaluating your situation.
### Step 3: Structure your voluntary savings plan on multiple levels
If your budget allows a positive free margin, allocate it strategically across multiple time horizons and risk levels:
1. Liquid emergency fund (3-6 months of essential expenses) on easily accessible bank account: protection from unexpected events 2. Pillar 3a ([pillar 3a](nav:pillar3)) — annual contributions tax-deductible up to about CHF 7,000 (employee) or CHF 20,000 (self-employed): tax-advantaged 3. Medium to long-term investments — stocks, bonds, funds, ETFs if you want to generate returns beyond simple liquidity: horizons >5 years 4. Supplementary pension protection — evaluate if your employer offers LPP/BVG with generous rates in coordination
In 2025, Swiss people set aside almost CHF 18,000 per person on average: approximately CHF 12,600 of these are voluntary savings (choice, not obligation). This capacity is historical and reflects real solidity if supported by conscious strategies.
### Step 4: Monitor variables that erode the savings margin
Even if nominal disposable income grows according to UST, three concrete factors continue to compress real savings and purchasing power:
- Inflation: even net of inflation (as UST data does), the psychological perception of costs remains high and strains budgets - Health premiums: grow on average faster than income in many cantons, eroding the available margin year after year - **Rent and real estate**: the Swiss market weighs increasingly on household finances, especially in areas of economic attraction
Review your personal plan each year when you receive your [payslip](nav:payslip) in January (first useful income of the year) and your [health insurance](nav:health) statements and tax notifications. These time triggers align with concrete decisions.
### What to do concretely in the coming weeks
1. Compare [health insurance](nav:health) options available in your canton of residence — premiums vary up to 30% between companies, with identical mandatory coverage 2. Open a [dedicated savings account](nav:banks) with positive interest rate (still rare in Switzerland in 2026, but a few institutions offer it) 3. ## At a glance - Top performers receive a 3.9% increase, nearly double the average (2%) - WTW: 97% of Swiss companies use performance metrics - In the IT sector, growth stalls at just 0.2% in 2026 - Estimated average of 2.3% in 2026, forecast of 2.4% in 2027
## Key facts - **What**: Annual survey on the structure of salary increases in Switzerland - When: 2026 (survey conducted this year) - Where: Switzerland, with particular focus on the IT sector - Who: WTW (business consulting firm) and SwissICT (IT industry association) - Amount: 3.9% (top performers), 2.0% (average), 0.8% (below average) - Key figure: 97% of companies consider performance in salary increases - Forecast: 2.4% estimated average increase for 2027
According to WTW's annual survey, salaries in Switzerland are increasingly differentiated based on work performance. This year, so-called top performers received increases of 3.9%, nearly double their colleagues with average performance, who received 2.0%. Employees with below-minimum performance received just 0.8%.
The companies surveyed by WTW attributed an average salary increase of 2.3%. The forecast for 2027 is slightly more optimistic: an average increase of 2.4% is estimated.
Differentiating salaries based on performance is now established practice in the Swiss business landscape: 97% of companies that apply individual increases explicitly consider personal performance, as shown in WTW's publication «Salary Budget Planning Report».
### Limited differences between hierarchical levels
WTW's report highlights an interesting finding: differences between various organizational levels remain contained. Managers do not automatically receive higher percentage adjustments compared to lower-level employees. Average increases for all employee groups move within a narrow band, ranging from 2.0% for lower levels to 2.3% for top management. This suggests that individual performance matters more than the role held in the organization.
To calculate the real impact of a salary increase on your net income, [use our salary calculator](nav:calculator), which takes into account federal, cantonal taxes and pension contributions according to your canton of residence. ### The collapse of the post-pandemic boom: the impact on the IT sector
A drastically different picture emerges from the IT sector. According to a report released by SwissICT, the Swiss industry association for the sector, salary growth is shrinking drastically. In 2026, the median salary in the IT sector grew by only 0.2%, a collapse when compared to previous years of sustained expansion.
The end of the post-pandemic boom marked a sharp fracture in the ICT market. Where previously there was widespread and almost automatic salary growth, today specialized skills and individual qualification matter most. The experts cited in the report explain that the sector is suffering the direct impact of artificial intelligence: the technology is transforming the mix of required skills, making some profiles less desirable and others—such as specialists in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and cybersecurity—even more sought after by the market.
### Who benefits and who falls behind
In this scenario of contraction, only the most qualified professionals can still hope for substantial salary increases. For most workers in the IT sector, salary adjustments are destined to remain extremely modest. This polarization reflects a broader trend in the Swiss economy: the distance between top performers and the masses is widening, both in the IT sector and in other sectors.
Those living and working in Switzerland, especially in the technology sector, are facing a reality transformed compared to the previous five years. Companies no longer distribute uniform salary gains: merit clearly rewards, but competition for specialized resources is fierce. An employee with standard skills will increasingly find it difficult to negotiate significant raises, while those who specialize still see opportunities for salary growth.
### Inflation reduces the impact of increases
Given that increases remain modest (average 2.3%), it is crucial to verify whether your own salary can offset the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living), which remains among the highest in the world. Rent, health insurance premiums, energy, and essential goods absorb a significant share of income. A 2.3% increase may not be enough to maintain real purchasing power, especially if you received 0.2% in the IT sector.

If you have received a raise or are about to negotiate a new salary, WTW data provides a useful benchmark for 2026. A median national increase stands at 2.3%. If you fall into the 'top performer' category according to company metrics (high ratings, exceptional results, specialized skills), expect an average increase around 3.9%. If your results are average, 2.0% is the reference figure. If your performance is below average, you stay at 0.8%.
These benchmarks apply to almost all Swiss companies: 97% apply performance criteria in determining increases. If your company does not clearly communicate the assignment criteria, or if you receive an increase below your performance level, you have reason to request a review meeting with the human resources management.
### Strategies in the Swiss labor market
For Swiss workers, especially those who do not fall into the top performer category, some practical implications emerge.
Specialization: investing in continuous training is essential. In the IT sector the trend is clear, but it applies to all sectors. Companies pay more for those with rare and hard-to-replace skills, and this gap tends to widen over time.
Professional mobility: if your employer offers increases below the category average (below 0.8%-2.0%), consider actively seeking new employment. The Swiss labor market remains dynamic, especially for specialists with required skills.
Transparent negotiation: document your results and performance. Companies that apply transparent metrics should be able to explain why you fall into one category rather than another. If the numbers do not match your assessment, ask for a meeting.
Supplementary pension: since salary increases remain modest, consider additional contributions to the [third pillar (3a)](nav:pillar3) to prepare for an adequate retirement. The AVS alone, especially for those with below-average salaries, may not guarantee sufficient income in the long term.

## In brief

## Key Facts

Switzerland's machinery, electrical engineering and metal industry (MEM) continues to face a difficult economic situation, but shows the first signs of recovery after months of tension. In the third quarter of 2026, the industry's economic climate index rose to -20 points, marking an improvement of 10 points compared to the previous three months. It is the best result since the beginning of spring 2024, according to a survey conducted by Swissmechanic, the industry association representing small and medium-sized enterprises in the sector.
However, the data should be interpreted with caution. According to the latest survey, 66 percent of companies surveyed still report an unfavorable economic situation. Only 34 percent express a positive assessment of their current conditions. We are not yet seeing a lasting reversal of the trend: the last time the indicator was in positive territory was April 2023, over three years earlier.
### Concrete signs of recovery
Nevertheless, the underlying indicators suggest that something is changing in the Swiss industrial fabric. Exports have been growing for the fourth consecutive quarter, a sign that international markets are beginning to absorb Swiss MEM products again. At the same time, the degree of production capacity utilization has returned to the long-term average for the first time since the end of 2023. A significant aspect: the use of reduced working hours, a crucial tool during economic crises, has declined considerably. With a recovery in productivity, salaries and compensation for people employed in the sector could also benefit from improvements—you can verify how this impacts your salaries with the [Swiss salary calculator](nav:calculator).
'Our companies demonstrate once again their resilience,' comments Nicola Tettamanti, president of Swissmechanic and CEO of Tecnopinz in Mezzovico (in Ticino). 'The first positive signs are encouraging: however, a lasting reversal of the trend requires stable general economic policy conditions and reliable prospects for our SMEs.' ### The challenge of the Swiss labour market
However, the economic recovery of the MEM sector cannot be separated from human capital. While concerns about the ordering situation diminish slightly, the shortage of specialized personnel is once again assuming central importance in company strategies. One in three companies (about 33 percent) consider this as one of the main challenges they face in the short and medium term.
The topic of vocational training acquires for the first time a strategic importance in Swissmechanic's economic barometer. Approximately two thirds of the companies surveyed (66 per cent) now recognise vocational training as an essential component of their personnel management strategy. It is not a given: until a few quarters ago, the focus of companies was mainly on reducing costs and preserving existing employment. 'Those who invest today in vocational training secure their specialized personnel for tomorrow,' concludes Erich Sannemann, director of Swissmechanic. The message is clear: MEM sector companies that intend to consolidate their recovery and prepare for sustainable growth must immediately tackle the challenges of recruitment and training.

## Key facts - **What**: revenue growth in the Swiss construction sector - When: first half of 2026 vs first half of 2025 - Where: Switzerland, communicated from Berne (SSIC) - Who: Swiss Association of Construction Entrepreneurs (SSIC) - Amount: CHF 11.2 billion - Revenue growth: +3.1% compared to the same period in 2025 - New orders growth: +1.6% to CHF 12.2 billion
In the first half of 2026, the Swiss construction sector continues to show clear growth, with revenue of CHF 11.2 billion, up 3.1% compared to the same period in 2025. The Swiss Association of Construction Entrepreneurs (SSIC) announced today from Berne that demand for new homes continues to drive the sector strongly. In detail, new orders rose 1.6% to CHF 12.2 billion on an annual basis.
Sectoral analysis reveals, however, very different dynamics. Residential construction shows a marked +8.1%, reaching CHF 4.1 billion: this is where the sector is concentrating its drive, with residential projects responding to growing demand for new homes. On the contrary, civil engineering works (railways, roads, bridges, infrastructure) record a decline of 2.1%, settling at CHF 4.8 billion. On the public-private front, the private sector signals growth of 5.4% to CHF 7.0 billion, while the public sector falls 0.5% to CHF 4.2 billion.
### Housing: urgent demand, construction slowed down
The SSIC estimates that during 2026, 48,000 new homes could be built, a considerable volume that testifies to national construction commitment. However, progress remains slowed by complex bureaucratic obstacles:
> In the first half, the main construction sector gained momentum. In 2026, 48,000 new homes could be built of which there is urgent need. Complex planning and building authorization procedures, as well as opposition and legal challenges, continue to slow down residential and infrastructure projects.
These 48,000 annual homes represent a significant effort to solve the housing shortage in Switzerland, an issue relevant to the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) and housing availability at federal and cantonal levels. But each individual residential project must navigate complex authorization procedures at the municipal and cantonal levels, often subject to disputes and appeals that lengthen implementation times. Opposition from local communities can indeed block or significantly delay construction sites. ### Civil engineering: waiting for "Transport '45"
If the housing construction runs, the civil genius remains stationary. The SSIC points out that the sector is in a stalemate due to uncertainty over infrastructure investments. In particular, the consultation of the "Transport '45" project, that is, the federal program of the next major phases of strengthening the national rail and road network, will end on October 9. Until the political process progresses further in the Federal Parliament and cantonal procedures, business builders struggle to plan new construction sites for roads and railways.
The situation on railway maintenance is even more critical. According to the SSIC, much more maintenance and renovation would be needed on existing lines, but personnel and financial resources are too limited. This means that Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) and cantonal railway operators do not have sufficient budgets and staff to properly maintain and modernise the network. A shortage that indirectly affects the quality of service and travel times for commuters who use public transport.

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to Navigate the Construction Boom and Delayed Construction Sites
For Swiss businesses, municipalities, and citizens, SSIC data paints a two-speed scenario. On one hand, residential construction offers concrete opportunities: if you're looking for a job in the construction sector, the 48,000 apartments planned for 2026 entail significant demand for laborers, craftspeople, designers, surveyors, and specialists. Construction companies are hiring and seeking qualified labor. You can check the [job listings in construction and engineering](nav:jobs) to explore available opportunities.
On the other hand, anyone planning to carry out a private residential project (single-family home, small residential complex) must prepare for lengthy authorization procedures at the municipal and cantonal levels. The solution is to inform yourself beforehand with your municipality about local procedures and average authorization timelines before starting the project.
For municipalities, the figure of 48,000 apartments represents both an opportunity and a responsibility. On one hand, more construction means higher tax revenue (property taxes, construction fees). On the other hand, municipalities must ensure adequate infrastructure (aqueducts, sewers, internal roads). Conscious territorial planning is essential to avoid congestion.

At the federal level, the 'Transport '45' project remains the fundamental lever for unlocking investments in railways and roads. ## In a nutshell - The Federal Council implements the IPG amendments from 1 July 2027 - Parents will be entitled to benefits hitherto reserved for military and civil service personnel - Four concrete measures: company allowances, prolonged maternity, bereavement, hospitalisation assistance

The Federal Council decided on 26 August 2026 to give the green light to the amendments to the law on loss of earnings indemnities, approved by Parliament in December 2025. The measures will come into force on 1 July 2027 and aim to harmonise benefits between parents and those performing military, civil or civil protection service.
Until today, those who take parental leave funded through loss of earnings compensation (IPG) did not have access to certain ancillary benefits, such as company allowances, childcare allowances, or bereavement allowances. These rights were reserved exclusively for military, civilian and civil protection volunteers. The new regulation eliminates this disparity.

Amendments to the IPG Act mainly affect parents who are entitled to parental leave funded through loss of earnings allowances. Until 1 July 2027, the situation was fragmented: parents and military/civilians enjoyed different protections despite being in comparable circumstances of loss of income.
With the reform, mothers and fathers who are absent from work due to parenthood will be able to access the same benefits as those on military or civil leave. Childcare allowances will compensate for the costs of babysitting or [asilo nido](nav:nursery) necessary to allow a parent to return to work after maternity.

## In a nutshell - Federal Council lowers LAINF threshold: from CHF 66,690 to CHF 44,460 per year from 1 January 2027 - 40,000 more independent workers can be insured - Easy access for low-income sectors, part-time women, cultural professionals
## Key facts - **What**: Review of accident insurance ordinance (OAINF) - When: Decision 26 August 2026; effective 1 January 2027 - Where: Switzerland (federal law) - Who: Federal Council - New threshold: CHF 44.460/anno (30% of the ceiling) - Previous threshold: CHF 66.690/anno (45% of the ceiling) - Beneficiaries: ~ 40,000 self-employed
Bern, 26 August 2026. The Federal Council has adopted a revision of the Ordinance on Accident Insurance (OAINF) to make coverage more accessible to self-employed workers. The decision significantly lowers the threshold for access to optional insurance, a move that allows around 40,000 more self-employed people to insure themselves from 1 January 2027.
The new threshold goes from CHF 66,690 per annum (45% of the amount of the maximum gain insured under the federal law LAINF) to CHF 44,460 per annum (30% of the same amount). This reduction is not just a technical detail, but a structural change of the Swiss accident risk protection system for the self-employed.
In Switzerland, the system is already well outlined for employees. All employees benefit from insurance The lowering of the threshold represents a concrete step forward for Swiss social protection of the self-employed. To understand the impact, just consider the figures: 40,000 more workers, so far excluded from the possibility of covering against the risk of injury. These are not abstract numbers, but people whose independent income is between CHF 44,460 and CHF 66,690 per year.
### Who will benefit from the new threshold
Lower-income professional sectors will benefit the most. Think of service freelancers, junior consultants, skilled artisans, cultural educators and private teachers who often struggle to reach standardized protection thresholds on employees with stable salaries, in the face of [costi della vita in Svizzera](nav:cost-of-living)s that remain high.
Women working part-time represent another crucial category. In Switzerland, part-time is still predominantly 'pink': women who have young children, who stack freelance jobs with salaried jobs, who manage self-employed projects alongside main part-time jobs. For them, the federal accident protection system has often remained unattainable precisely because of the high threshold. With the new limit, many more professionals will have access to basic coverage. If you are a part-time mom, you can deepen your [diritti in materia di congedo parentale](nav:parental-leave) and social protection, which integrate with this new injury opportunity.
The cultural sector deserves a separate mention.

The new ordinance comes into force on January 1, 2027. ### How to Proceed
The first step is to verify whether you fall within the new access threshold. The threshold is CHF 44,460 of annual income (or 30% of the maximum amount of CHF 148,200 set by the LAINF). If your self-employed income is between CHF 44,460 and CHF 66,690, you will be a beneficiary of the new regulation and will be able to subscribe to optional insurance for the first time. If you were already earning CHF 66,690, your position does not formally change, but it is advisable to check whether the premiums offered by various insurers will change following the reduction of the threshold.
The second step is to contact Swiss insurers operating in the LAINF accident insurance sector. Among the main players are SUVA, AXA, Generali and other companies offering this type of coverage. There is no single federal portal: each insurer has its own forms, processing times and conditions. It is advisable to explicitly ask whether they accept customers below the previous threshold, since from January 1, 2027 the regulation changes, but the administrative transition may have variable timelines.
The third step concerns the cultural sector and part-time professionals with multiple activities. Clarify with the insurer how your activity rate is calculated if you simultaneously hold a dependent employment position and self-employed activity. The new flexibility provided in the ordinance allows insurers to adjust the threshold calculation based on the actual percentage of self-employed activity compared to the total. If you work 40% as an employee and 60% as self-employed, for example, the insurer might consider only 60% of your income for threshold calculation. This is an advantage over the previous system, but requires clear communication with the provider.
### Documentation and Deadlines
When you contact an insurer, prepare documentation relating to your self-employed income from recent years (balance sheets, tax returns, or alternatively a certified estimate of expected income for the current year). Insurers will assess your request and communicate whether the threshold calculation makes you eligible. There is no rigid federal deadline for subscriptions, but it is advisable to contact insurers by November 2026 to ensure coverage activation starting January 1, 2027.

item.title: Open activities in Appenzello Interno: costs and register
item.description: Legal form, registration in the commercial register, three-tier taxation and insurance: this is what you need to start a business in the canton.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Switzerland applies a tax system at three levels: federal, cantonal and municipal - Registration in the commercial register is mandatory before starting the activity - The legal form chosen affects minimum capital, liabilities and obligations - Social security contributions (AVS, LPP) are mandatory for all entrepreneurs
## Key facts - **What**: Registration of commercial activity with the cantonal authorities - Where: Inner Appenzell Canton (trade register office) - Who: Owners of sole proprietorships, simple companies, SAGL, public limited companies - Time: The procedure takes 1-2 weeks from the complete presentation of the documentation - Costs: Vary according to legal form and canton
Starting a business in Switzerland requires compliance with precise procedures defined at federal and cantonal level. In the Inner Appenzell canton, as in the other Swiss cantons, the first step is to choose the legal form that best suits your business project. The decision between a sole proprietorship, simple company, limited liability company (SAGL), public limited company (SA) or cooperative is not purely formal: it conditions personal liability, the minimum capital required, the tax structure and advertising obligations.
A sole proprietorship, the simplest form, does not require a minimum capital defined by law, but implies full personal responsibility of the entrepreneur towards the ### Three-level taxation: federal, cantonal and municipal Switzerland applies a multi-level tax system that directly affects every entrepreneur. At the federal level, there is the Federal Direct Tax (IFD) on business income, managed by the Federal Customs Administration (FCA). At the cantonal level, the canton of Appenzell Rhodes-Iodine applies a business income tax according to its own legal rates, which can vary significantly from one canton to another. At the municipal level, individual municipalities multiply the cantonal rate to obtain the final municipal rate: this multiplier mechanism means that two companies in the same canton, but in different municipalities, pay slightly different taxes.
Furthermore, all companies subject to turnover tax above a certain threshold must register for Value Added Tax (VAT), administered at the federal level. The standard VAT rate is 7.7%, but reduced rates of 2.5% for food items and 3.7% for pharmaceuticals and newspapers exist. VAT registration becomes mandatory with annual turnover exceeding a level defined by federal law; below that, registration is optional but convenient if the company has many B2B clients.
### Mandatory pension systems and insurance For all entrepreneurs who personally conduct a business activity, contributions to the state pension system are mandatory. The AVS (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance) requires a contribution on business income calculated differently than for employees: the rate is progressive and calculated on the company's net income. [Professional pension](nav:pension) (LPP) is mandatory when the company has employees: the employer must pay contributions on behalf of employees, with percentages varying according to the employee's age (ages 25 to 34: 7% of coordinated salary, with increasing percentages up to 18% for those 55 years and older).
The AVS/AI/IPG contribution rate for employees is 5.3% for the employee and 10.6% in total with the employer (the employer pays both shares). Contributions for unemployment insurance (AD) and accident insurance (AC) complete the picture: AD is 1.1% up to an annual maximum, while AC varies from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector of activity.
As for health insurance (LAMal), it is mandatory for every Swiss resident within three months of arrival or registration of the activity. It is not a tax, but private insurance whose premiums vary by canton and region. The canton of Appenzell Rhodes-Iodine offers premium reductions (subsidies) for low-income families, managed by the cantonal administration.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Practical Step-by-Step Procedure The first step is to consult the commercial register office of the canton Appenzell Inner Rhodes to learn about the exact local requirements, the forms to fill out, and the applicable fees. The standard procedure includes: choosing a legal form and drafting, where necessary, a statute or partnership agreement (it is advisable to seek legal or notarial consultation for SA and SAGL); opening a bank account dedicated to the business; completing the registration application for the commercial register with all required documents (identity document, bank account statement, criminal record extracts if required, certificate of good conduct where required); payment of the registration fee (amount varies by canton); waiting for approval and publication in the official cantonal journal.
After registration with the commercial register, the entrepreneur must register with the federal social security authorities. This means contacting the competent AVS office for the place of residence and submitting a registration application, indicating the estimated business income. For companies with employees, it is mandatory to affiliate with a recognized LPP compensation fund and to take out accident insurance (LAINF/LAA) with SUVA or an authorized private insurer.
### Registration Fees and Initial Costs Registration fees for the commercial register vary significantly depending on the canton and sometimes even by municipality. In the case of Appenzell Inner Rhodes, the exact amount must be verified with the competent office, since there is no uniform figure at the federal level. Similarly, if you choose a SAGL, it is necessary to deposit the minimum capital with a bank and provide a bank certificate; the same applies to an SA, which requires a higher minimum capital.
In addition to registration fees, it is advisable to budget for legal consultation costs (especially for SA and SAGL), bank fees for opening the business account, and the first installments of pension and insurance contributions. An entrepreneur with employees must also calculate the costs of LPP payments and accident insurance from the first month of operations.
### Next Operational Steps Once the business is launched, it is essential to maintain accounting according to Swiss standards (for sole proprietorships, simple accounting records are sufficient; for partnerships, full balance sheet and income statement). Annually, you must submit the [tax return](nav:tax-return) at the federal and cantonal level, and pay income tax according to the deadlines set by the administration. To better plan your business's tax and pension structure, use the [calculators dedicated to taxes and pension contributions](nav:calculator) available from federal and cantonal offices.

item.title: Opening a business in Appenzello Interno: a practical guide
item.description: Legal forms, minimum capital, trade register registration and tax, contribution and insurance obligations to start a business in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Switzerland requires precise legal forms: SA (CHF 100,000 capital), Sarl (CHF20,000), sole proprietorship without minimum - Each canton manages the trade register; tax competences divided between AFC/ESTV (federal/VAT) and cantonal administrations - Employees mean obligations: AVS/AI (5.3% employer + 5.3% employee), AD/AC (1.1%), SUVA work accidents, LAMal
## Key facts - **What**: Start a business in Switzerland with a choice of legal form and official registration with the cantonal administration - Legal forms: Company (no minimum capital), SA (CHF 100,000), Sarl (CHF20,000), Cooperative (variable) - Competences: AFC/ESTV for IFD and VAT; cantonal administrations for trade register and local taxes - Compulsory insurance: SUVA for accidents at work (employees), LAMal for health (per capita) - Social contributions: AVS/AI 5.3% + 5.3% employer, AD/AC 1.1% up to annual ceiling, LAINF/LAA 0.7–1.5% by sector, LPP 7–18% by age group
In Switzerland, starting a business is governed by coexisting federal and cantonal procedures. The Inner Appenzell Canton, like all other cantons, entrusts the local trade register with the task of formally registering the new company and coordinating tax obligations with the Federal Administration of Customs (AFC) and the Federal VAT Office (ESTV). The choice of legal form — sole proprietorship, public limited company (SA), company to The Swiss tax system operates on three overlapping levels: federal (FTA — Federal Direct Tax), cantonal, and municipal. It is not simple decentralization, but rather parallel and coordinated jurisdiction. The FTA/ESTV manages exclusively VAT and federal direct taxes; cantonal administrations manage cantonal and municipal taxes. The municipal multiplier varies from municipality to municipality: there is no single value for the entire Appenzell Innerrhoden, but each municipality sets it in accordance with cantonal law.
### Federal and Cantonal Tax Obligations
**VAT registration** becomes mandatory when annual turnover exceeds CHF 100,000. The FTA/ESTV requires online registration on the official federal administration portal. If turnover remains below this threshold, registration remains optional, but allows you to recover VAT on purchases; it is advisable to evaluate case by case.
The Federal Direct Tax (FDT) applies to the net income of the individual enterprise or corporation. For sole proprietorships and partnerships, profit is taxed to the owner at the federal, cantonal, and municipal level. For corporations (AG, GmbH), business profit is taxed to the company; any dividend to shareholders is subject to additional taxation (Swiss classical system, with exceptions for qualified shareholdings).
The Appenzell Innerrhoden cantonal administration sets its own cantonal and municipal tax rates. Since these values vary and are updated annually, it is essential to contact the cantonal tax office or the specific municipality to find out the current multipliers.
### Mandatory Insurance and Social Contributions
When you hire your first employee, mandatory contribution obligations are automatically triggered:
AHV/AI (Old-age, survivors' and disability insurance): the employer pays 5.3% on the employee's salary; the employee contributes a further 5.3%. This is a joint payment to the cantonal contribution office. It is mandatory for every employee, regardless of sector.
UI (Unemployment insurance): 1.1% of gross salary up to an established annual ceiling. Employer and employee contribute in equal measure.
WICA (Workplace accident insurance): mandatory for employees. The premium ranges from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector of activity. Higher-risk sectors (construction, mining, work at height) have higher rates. It is the employer's responsibility to register workers with a SUVA-approved insurer within the established deadlines.
LAMal/KVG (Mandatory health insurance): every resident in Switzerland must take out health insurance within 3 months of arrival. Premiums are per capita — they vary by canton and region — and are not deducted from the payslip but paid by the employee directly to the insurer. Deductibles for adults range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 annually. Many cantons provide [premium subsidies](nav:health) for incomes below a certain threshold.
LPP/BVG (Occupational pension fund): if the company employs employees with coordinated salary above a minimum threshold, registration with a pension fund is mandatory. Contributions vary by age group: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44), 15% (45–54), 18% (55+ until retirement age).
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). Opening a business in Switzerland follows a precise sequence. Here are the main steps to complete before operationally launching your company.
### Step 1: Choose legal form and verify name availability
Decide between sole proprietorship, SA, Sarl or cooperative based on size, desired liability and available capital. If you choose a business name, verify its availability at the cantonal commercial register: many cantons offer free online search. Make sure the name is not already registered and that it complies with any cantonal regulations on business names.
### Step 2: Prepare constitutional documentation
For SA and Sarl, draw up the bylaws (or articles of association) according to cantonal models or with the help of a notary. For sole proprietorship, the registration form is sufficient. If the business has multiple partners, it is advisable to draw up a partnership agreement that regulates rights, duties, exit criteria, and profit distribution.
### Step 3: Registration at the cantonal commercial register
Contact the commercial register office of your cantonal jurisdiction. Present: - Registration form (available at the office or online on the canton's website) - Bylaws or articles of association (for SA/Sarl) - Authenticated copy of the owner/partners' identity card - Financial documentation: bank statement or bank letter certifying the payment of minimum capital (for SA/Sarl) - Any commercial authorization if required by the sector (catering, pharmacy, hairdresser, etc.)
Registration generates a CHE number (company identification number). The commercial register automatically notifies the FTA/ESTV.
### Step 4: VAT registration (if applicable)
If your expected or actual turnover exceeds CHF 100,000 annually, register for VAT with the FTA/ESTV within 30 days of reaching the threshold. Registration is mandatory; delays result in penalties. Use the [tax calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate your federal tax burden and assess whether voluntary registration is worthwhile.
### Step 5: Declaration of activity with the tax authority
Contact the cantonal tax office to report the start of your business. You will receive guidance on declaration deadlines (usually annual) and payment methods. You will need an account number for periodic payments.
### Step 6: Registration for social insurance and contributions
Register with the cantonal contribution office (AVS/AI/AD/AC) and with a SUVA insurer for LAINF. Provide CHE number, list of employees with personal data and salaries, and business sector.
### Step 7: Conclusion of mandatory insurance
Ensure that each employee has LAMal (health insurance). If not yet taken out, the employee must do so within 3 months of their first day of work. Also consider obtaining **professional liability insurance** (not mandatory in all sectors, but strongly recommended to protect the company from compensation claims).
### Overall timeline
The process from documentation preparation to official registration generally takes 2–4 weeks. The registration fees for the commercial register vary from canton to canton and are not specified here; contact the cantonal administration directly for details.
### Daily management and recurring deadlines
Once operational, the company will have recurring deadlines: VAT declarations (quarterly or annual), federal and cantonal tax declaration (annual), social insurance data communication (annual), and financial statements (for SA/Sarl with possible audit). You must also comply with labor regulations: maximum 45–50 hours/week depending on the sector, minimum 4 weeks annual vacation (5 for employees under 20 years old), regular social contributions, and notice periods (1, 2 or 3 months depending on years of service).
If you hire foreign employees, verify residence permits with the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM): short-term permits (L), residence (B), domicile (C) or cross-border (G) have different regimes.
Use our [tax calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the tax burden of your newly opened business. To search for and contact employees in Switzerland, consult our [database of hiring companies](nav:companies).

item.title: AVS and complementary services in Appenzello Interno
item.description: First pillar in Inner Appenzell: guide to the compensation fund, calculation of the AVS annuity and complementary benefits for the minimum living.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The first pillar AVS is managed by the cantonal compensation fund of Appenzell Innerrhoden - Contribution gaps reduce the pension and are offset by complementary benefits - Complementary benefits protect the minimum living standard for the insured
## Key facts - **What**: first pillar (AVS/AHV) and minimum social protection - Where: Canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, Switzerland - Who: Federal UFAS/BSV, cantonal compensation fund, AVS insured persons - Function: pension calculation, coverage of contribution gaps, minimum living standard protection - Authority: federal management (UFAS/BSV) + cantonal administration
Appenzell Innerrhoden, like all 26 Swiss cantons, has a compensation fund that administers the first pillar, namely old-age, survivors' and disability insurance (AVS/AHV). The federal body that oversees the entire system is the Federal Office of Social Insurance (UFAS), also known as the Bureau of Social Insurance (BSV in German). The cantonal compensation fund of Appenzell Innerrhoden concretely manages the registration of new insured persons, the collection of mandatory contributions, the calculation of future pensions and, if necessary, the provision of complementary benefits. This federal system represents one of the pillars of Swiss social security and constitutes the basic social protection network for those who work and reside in Switzerland.
Each canton has its own compensation fund, but all operate according to the same federal rules laid down by the Federal Law on Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (LAVS/AVG). This means that the level of protection is identical throughout the national territory, even though the administrative bodies are local and decentralized.
### Structure and financing of the first pillar
The first pillar is financed by mandatory contributions calculated on salary. Employees contribute 5.3 percent of their remuneration, while the employer contributes another 5.3 percent, for a total of 10.6 percent. In addition to AVS/AHV, these contributions also cover disability insurance (AI) and loss-of-earnings benefits (IPG). Self-employed workers pay the contribution both from the employee side and (partly) from the employer side.
The AVS pension is calculated on the basis of the number of insurance years (years with contributions paid) and a formula that revalues past salaries according to the national average wage index. It is not a simple arithmetic average of earnings, but a more complex procedure that considers the level of income throughout the entire working life. However, if there are periods without contributions – the so-called contribution gaps – the pension will be lower than the maximum. In these cases, complementary benefits come into play, which guarantee anyone entitled to a pension a minimum capable of covering the vital minimum.
[Discover how the [Swiss pension system](nav:pension) works] Understanding how the AHV pension is calculated means knowing the system of credits in insurable years. It is not a simple salary average: the procedure is more sophisticated. Each contribution year is revalued according to the average development of national wages, so earnings from the 1990s are adjusted to current salary levels before being entered into the formula. The Federal Office of Social Insurance publishes updated pension tables each year to reflect Switzerland's economic and demographic dynamics. Anyone wishing to know their pension amount in advance can request an individual account statement – called an AHV account statement – from the competent compensation fund, in this case the one in Appenzell Innerrhoden. The service is free.
### Contribution Gaps and Their Concrete Impact
A contribution gap is a year (or more years) in which an insured person did not pay contributions. This can happen for various reasons: periods of unemployment not covered by unemployment insurance (AD/AC), years of study before age 20 not automatically recognized, career interruptions due to family or health reasons, or temporary emigration without contribution buyback. Each gap reduces the number of insurable years and therefore decreases the future pension. A person with 43 years of contributions will have a lower pension than someone with 44, even if their salaries were identical.
Supplementary benefits (SB) come into play when the sum of the AHV pension (first pillar) and occupational pension benefits, that is, the second pillar LPP/BVG, does not reach the minimum subsistence level set by federal law. The Appenzell Innerrhoden cantonal fund pays out the difference as a supplementary allowance, thus ensuring all retirees a dignified livelihood. This mechanism is essential for precarious, seasonal, or workers with fragmented careers: even if their pensions are low, they remain protected by a minimum threshold of pension income. Supplementary benefits are financed by the confederation and the cantons in proportion established by law.
[Use the [tax and pension calculator](nav:calculator) for a personalized estimate of your allowance]
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). If you reside in Appenzell Innerrhoden and are approaching retirement, the first concrete step is to verify your AVS account with the cantonal compensation office. You can request an account statement free of charge, a document that shows the number of insured years recognized, salaries recorded year by year, any gaps or discrepancies, and an estimate of the future pension based on current data.
### Procedure for access and verification of eligibility
The compensation office of Appenzell Innerrhoden accepts requests in writing or electronically. You will need to provide a copy of your identity document (passport, identity card), the account statement request form (available online on the UFAS/BSV portal), and a possible statement from your current employer if still employed. Processing time is usually 10–15 working days. Once you receive the account, you can verify the accuracy of the data, report any suspected errors or gaps, and calculate a projection of your pension with the help of a consultant at the office.
If you discover critical gaps, you can buy back missing contributions by paying a flat-rate amount calculated according to UFAS/BSV tables. This buyback increases your future pension and reduces reliance on supplementary benefits. Buyback is an important tool for those who have interrupted their career for documented reasons.
### How to access supplementary benefits
If after the final calculation your AVS pension plus that of the second pillar LPP does not reach the minimum subsistence level, you can submit an application for supplementary benefits to the compensation office of Appenzell Innerrhoden at the same time as your AVS pension application. It is not a separate phase: it is integrated into the ordinary process of granting the pension. The office will verify income from pensions and activities, movable and immovable assets, and family situation and dependents. Supplementary benefits will cover the difference up to the minimum subsistence level, guaranteeing a dignified and sustainable pension.

item.title: School and future: young people from Ticino are at risk of leaving
item.description: On August 31, school begins again in Ticino. But what future awaits young people after training? Salaries, rents and sick pay premiums put economic independence at risk.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - On August 31, Ticino schools begin again with thousands of students - Young people struggle to become financially independent after training - The Canton risks the flight of talent to other regions of Switzerland - Training alone is not enough without competitive salaries and opportunities
## Key facts - **What**: Back to school in Ticino for children and teenagers - When: Monday, August 31 - Where: Ticino (Italian-speaking Swiss canton) - Who: Thousands of students from Ticino schools - Central theme: Labour Market Preparation and Talent Retention - Challenges: Low salaries, high rents, sick pay premiums (LAMal), economic independence - Perspective: Connection between school education and concrete employment opportunities
### Back to school and the question of the future
On Monday, August 31, Ticino schools will reopen their doors and thousands of children and teenagers will return to the benches with new backpacks, fresh books and the enthusiasm (or reluctance) of every beginning of the year. But behind this ordinary chronicle hides a much more urgent question, posed by columnist Elio Del Biaggio: what future are we really preparing for our young people?
This is not a trivial question. Education, according to Del Biaggio, does not consist only in transmitting knowledge. It means preparing children for concrete life, work, responsibility and autonomy. It means providing the tools to deal with a rapidly changing world. And ### Vocational training as a key element
The columnist underlines an important point that is often underestimated in the public debate: professional training (apprenticeship) is not a "series B" option for those who cannot afford or do not want to do higher education. A qualified apprenticeship can be a concrete and fast door to the labour market, with real career prospects and competitive salaries.
In this sense, the school has a dual responsibility: not only to transmit theoretical knowledge and technical skills, but also to restore social and economic value to the diversity of training courses. When a young person perceives that apprenticeship is seen as an inferior choice, they are less motivated to pursue it with commitment. On the contrary, if society (and the school) clearly communicates that this is also a legitimate and quality path, it increases the likelihood that the young person will develop concrete skills and find work more quickly.
### Skills that are missing in the real world
Del Biaggio focuses attention on what he calls the "real world": young people leave school, but are often unprepared for rapid changes in the labour market. Professions are evolving, and digital skills are becoming central to almost every industry. Continuing education (career retraining) is increasingly necessary to stay competitive.
The school, therefore, should
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### What must change in Ticino schools
The editorialist implicitly proposes a paradigm shift in education. Schools must continue to transmit solid knowledge, but they must also become a bridge between the theoretical world and the world of concrete work. This means preparing young people for professions that are constantly changing, emphasizing digital skills not as optional but as an essential part of any educational path, teaching that learning does not end with a diploma but is a continuous process, clearly valuing apprenticeships as a legitimate and quality path, and developing transversal skills that remain critical regardless of technology.
But all of this is secondary if the fundamental is missing: instilling in young people the confidence that their future can be built in Ticino, that merit truly matters, that opportunities exist and are concrete. Without this fundamental confidence, even the best school in the world will not retain talent.
Every year, when school starts again, the reflection should not be limited to 'what will our young people learn?'. It should include with equal weight: 'What will they find when they graduate? What job opportunities? What realistic salaries? What quality of life will they be able to afford given the current cost of living?'.
### The concrete cost of living for young people
Young people from Ticino who complete their training must face a precise economic reality. It is not just about generic salary: you must subtract from that gross salary the mandatory contributions (AVS/AI, LPP/pension, accident insurance), federal, cantonal and municipal taxes, the [concrete cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) (rising rents, [health insurance](nav:health) premiums via LAMal, food, transportation, utilities).
For what appears to be a good salary, if not supported by conscious management and real information, economic independence can remain a mirage. Hence the importance of guiding young people to understand from the start what the true cost of living in Ticino is and how to build a realistic budget.
### If the answers remain uncertain
If the answers to questions about the future remain uncertain or discouraging, no headline about excellent education will stop the brain drain. And Ticino, as other European regions have already experienced, risks losing entire generations of competent young people, full of ambitions and energy.

## In a nutshell - Maximum security deposit of 3 months of rent on a restricted account in the name of the tenant - Dispute of the fee within 30 days to the cantonal conciliation authority - Cancellation in writing, with terms 1/2/3 months second year of contract - Uniform federal regulations (CO art. 253 et seq.) valid in each canton including Appenzell Inner
## Key facts - **What**: Federal Residential Lease Regulations - Legal basis: Swiss Civil Code, art. 253 et seq. - Where: All Swiss cantons, including Inner Appenzell - Deposit ceiling: 3 months of rent on a restricted account - Fee dispute deadline: 30 days from written notice - Form of cancellation: Written (letter, registered letter, fax, email) - Cancellation notice: 1 month (1st year), 2 months (2nd-9th year), 3 months (from 10th year)
The rental market in Switzerland is governed by uniform federal provisions that apply regardless of the canton of residence. In the canton of Appenzello Interno, as in all other cantons, leases for residential properties are governed by federal law (CO art. 253 et seq.), which sets identical rules for security deposits, dispute fees and cancellation proceedings.
### Security deposit: restrictions and protection
The first practical issue a tenant faces is the security deposit. Federal law limits the deposit to a maximum of three months' rent. This amount cannot ### Dispute procedures and fee increase
When a tenant disputes the rent, the first step is to document the position with market comparisons: similar rentals in the area, data published on real estate portals, local valuations. This documentation provides the basis for the appeal submitted to the cantonal conciliation authority. The authority examines the data and proposes a mediation; if it does not reach agreement, it orders an independent appraisal to calculate the rent in accordance with the market. The procedure is generally concluded within 60-90 days.
Federal law allows the landlord to increase the rent only when two conditions are met: the consumer price index (CPI, published by the Federal Statistical Office UST/BFS) has risen by at least 5% since the previous rent increase, or the costs of managing and maintaining the property have increased documented. Any increase that does not meet these criteria is illegitimate and objectionable using the same mechanism (appeal within 30 days to the conciliation authority).
### Cancellation of the contract: written forms and binding terms
**Cancellation** follows strict rules. A verbal, message, chat or telephone cancellation has no legal effect. Written support is mandatory: it can be a paper letter sent by ordinary mail, registered letter, fax, or email, as long as the content is legible and clearly attributable to the sender. Written support
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What to do concretely: step-by-step operational guide
If you are signing a rental contract in Appenzell Innerrhoden or any other Swiss canton, follow this procedure:
Step 1 — Verify the security deposit: Check that the payment is made to a blocked account in your name at an authorized bank or financial institution. The account number must be communicated in writing by the landlord. Never hand over cash, checks, or transfers to ordinary current accounts. If the landlord requests different methods, refuse and report to the conciliation authority.
Step 2 — Receive and keep the contract in written form: The contract must contain the monthly rent, start date, duration (if determined), payment method, and property location. Keep the original. If the rent appears unjustifiably high compared to the area, start counting 30 days from receipt to file an appeal.
Step 3 — File an appeal if the rent is contestable: Contact the cantonal conciliation authority office of Appenzell Innerrhoden (name and contact details available on the cantonal administrative website). Request official forms and submission procedures. Attach documentation on comparable rents in the area: listings, agency valuations, public data. Submit the written appeal within 30 days of receiving the contract.
Step 4 — Participate in the conciliation procedure: The authority will summon you together with the landlord. Present your documentary material. If no agreement is reached, the authority orders an independent technical appraisal (usually at the applicant's expense, but sometimes free if the appeal is well-founded).
Step 5 — Terminate the contract (if you decide to move): Calculate your desired exit date. If you are in the first year, send a written notice at least 30 days in advance. If you are in the second to ninth year, at least 60 days in advance. If you are in the tenth year or beyond, at least 90 days in advance. Preferably send it by registered mail with return receipt, so you have proof of sending and a certain date. Continue paying rent until the notice period expires.
Step 6 — Return the property and recover the deposit: Empty and clean the apartment by the expiration date. The landlord has 30 days from taking possession of the property to inspect it, identify damage, and communicate deductions from the deposit (damage, unpaid rent, extraordinary maintenance). The remaining balance of the deposit must be transferred to your current account.
### Useful tools and resources
To assess whether the proposed rent is consistent with the regional context, consult nav:cost-of-living — the tool takes into account average rental prices by canton and region. If you are changing jobs and cantons, check the opportunities available on [nav:jobs](nav:jobs) to plan your move in advance and comply with legal notice periods. For questions about tax deductions related to rental expenses (some cantons allow partial deductions), consult nav:tax-return when completing your annual tax return.
